stream = h2o_http2_stream_open(conn, frame->stream_id, NULL, &payload.priority);
set_priority(conn, stream, &payload.priority, 0);
anchors.note: Source. The HEADERS frame in the first PoC packet creates stream 13 and opens its `_scheduler` reference in the connection dependency tree. This is the first project state that later survives into the preserved closed-stream stub.

The same HEADERS frame carries `END_STREAM`, so this condition is false and `h2o_buffer_init` is skipped. Because `h2o_http2_stream_open()` zeroed the newly allocated stream prefix before `req`, `_req_body.body` stays `NULL` on stream 13.
Because `_req_body.body` is still `NULL`, the complete HEADERS-only request is executed immediately instead of moving into `RECV_BODY`.

Request handling reaches H2O's send path for stream 13. `finalostream_send()` moves the stream into its outbound state, stores any queued response iovecs in `_data`, and then requests write scheduling for that live stream.

The live outbound stream is made active in the HTTP/2 scheduler only after `assert(!h2o_linklist_is_linked(&stream->_link))` proves `_link` is unlinked. `h2o_http2_scheduler_activate()` then sets `_self_is_active = 1` and increments the active counts that later get preserved incorrectly.
Later in the same first packet, the WINDOW_UPDATE frame for stream 13 decodes to increment 0. The decoder marks that as a stream-level protocol error because `frame->stream_id != 0`.

The invalid zero-increment WINDOW_UPDATE is handled as a stream-level error on the already active stream 13, so H2O immediately calls `h2o_http2_stream_reset(conn, stream)` on that live outbound stream.

Because the stream was already in a sending state, reset first advances it to `END_STREAM`, clears queued body count, and then takes the immediate `h2o_http2_stream_close` branch because step 5 established that `_link` is unlinked.

Before unregistering the stream, H2O allocates a shortened ring-buffer entry for recently closed priorities. This object intentionally retains only `stream_id` and `_scheduler`; fields after `_scheduler`, including `_data`, do not exist in this allocation.

Root cause site. The close path preserves the active scheduler inside the truncated closed-stream stub and then returns to finish closing the original stream. Vulnerable code leaves the relocated scheduler active here; the patch adds an immediate deactivation after this call.

The relocate helper copies the live scheduler state into the stub verbatim: the active count, the `_self_is_active` bit, and the queued WRR link all move to `dst`. The preserved closed-stream stub therefore stays runnable in the scheduler even though it is no longer a full `h2o_http2_stream_t`.

When the connection later runs the scheduler, the preserved closed-stream entry is still marked active, so `proceed()` invokes the write callback on that stub instead of treating it as an inactive interior node.

The callback blindly reconstructs a full `h2o_http2_stream_t *` from the active scheduler reference. After steps 9-11, `ref` actually points into the shortened recently-closed-stream allocation, not a complete live stream object.

Sink. `_data` lives after `_scheduler` in the real stream struct, but the preserved object from step 9 stops at `_scheduler`. Evaluating this expression therefore performs the saved 8-byte heap out-of-bounds read beyond the truncated closed-stream stub.
